Introduction

Marriage is not merely a contract between consenting adults; it is a foundational social institution with deep roots in human biology, civilization, and moral tradition. The Obergefell decision was decided 5–4 by an unelected panel of judges. Justice Antonin Scalia's dissent warned that the Court had short-circuited this democratic process, imposing a single answer on a deeply contested moral and social question.

II. The Institutional Argument: Marriage's Unique Purpose

Proponents of traditional marriage argue that the institution exists primarily because of a biological reality: heterosexual unions produce children. The case for restoring traditional marriage rests on democratic legitimacy, the unique procreative purpose of marriage, protection of religious liberty, cultural coherence, and sound constitutional interpretation. Restoring Marriage: A Case for Returning to the Traditional Legal Definition

Introduction

In Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), the Supreme Court of the United States, by a narrow 5-4 majority, declared a constitutional right to same-sex marriage. This decision, while celebrated by many, represented one of the most consequential acts of judicial overreach in modern American jurisprudence. The ruling short-circuited a democratic process that was properly unfolding across the fifty states, imposed a singular moral vision on a diverse republic, and redefined an institution whose meaning had been understood across civilizations for millennia. This essay argues that the legal definition of marriage should be restored to the union of one man and one woman — not out of malice toward any person, but out of fidelity to constitutional governance, the integrity of institutions, the welfare of children, and the principles of democratic self-determination.

I. Constitutional Legitimacy and the Problem of Judicial Overreach

The most foundational argument for reversing Obergefell is not about marriage itself — it is about the Constitution and who has authority to define fundamental social institutions.

A. The Absence of Textual or Historical Grounding

The Constitution nowhere mentions marriage. The Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, were plainly enacted to secure the civil rights of freed slaves and to ensure basic legal equality before the law. No legislator who voted for the Fourteenth Amendment, no citizen who ratified it, and no jurist who interpreted it for over a century understood it to require the redefinition of marriage. As Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in his Obergefell dissent:

> "The majority's decision is an act of will, not legal judgment. The right it announces has no basis in the Constitution or this Court's precedent."

If constitutional rights are to have stable meaning, they must be grounded in text, history, and structure — not in evolving moral preferences of a shifting majority of nine unelected justices. The doctrine of "substantive due process," under which Obergefell was decided, has been among the most criticized and abused doctrines in constitutional law. It was the same doctrine that produced Dred Scott v. Sandford and Lochner v. New York — decisions now universally regarded as catastrophic errors where the Court substituted its policy preferences for law.

B. The Theft of Democratic Self-Governance

At the time of Obergefell, the democratic process was actively working. Several states had legalized same-sex marriage through legislation or popular vote. Others had declined to do so. This is precisely how a federal republic is designed to function — allowing diverse communities to reach different conclusions on contested moral questions through deliberation, persuasion, and consent.

The Court's intervention did not resolve a debate; it terminated one. It told the citizens of every state that had voted to preserve traditional marriage — often by overwhelming margins — that their democratic participation was meaningless. Justice Scalia warned in his dissent that the decision represented a threat "to American democracy," noting that the Court had effectively removed an issue of profound moral significance from the hands of the people and their elected representatives.

A self-governing people must be permitted to define the institutions at the heart of their common life. Restoring the traditional definition of marriage through proper democratic or constitutional channels would not be an act of regression but a reassertion of popular sovereignty and constitutional fidelity.

II. Marriage as a Pre-Political Institution Oriented Toward Procreation

A. The Conjugal View of Marriage

For thousands of years, across virtually every civilization, religion, and legal tradition, marriage has been understood as a conjugal institution — a comprehensive union of man and woman oriented by its nature toward the bearing and raising of children. This understanding was not the invention of any single religion or culture; it was recognized by ancient Roman law, Confucian tradition, English common law, African customary practice, Hindu tradition, and Islamic jurisprudence alike. Its cross-cultural universality reflects something deeper than mere convention.

The conjugal view holds that marriage is unique because it unites two people in a relationship that is, by its biological nature, the kind of union that produces new life. No other human relationship has this character. The state has historically recognized and regulated marriage not because it wished to validate romantic feelings — the state has no particular interest in certifying emotional attachments — but because the sexual union of men and women produces children, and children need stable, committed families.

B. The Public Purpose of Marriage Law

The essential question is: Why does the state involve itself in marriage at all? The government does not certify best friendships or issue licenses for deep emotional bonds. The state's interest in marriage has always been connected to its interest in responsible procreation and the welfare of the next generation.

When a man and a woman conceive a child, that child has a mother and a father. Marriage is the institution that binds those parents to each other and to their offspring, creating a framework of mutual obligation before the child is even born. Same-sex relationships, whatever their personal value to the individuals involved, do not — and cannot, by nature — produce children from both partners. Extending the legal framework of marriage to relationships that lack this procreative character fundamentally changes what marriage is in the eyes of the law. It transforms marriage from an institution centered on children's needs into one centered on adult desires for recognition.

Scholars Sherif Girgis, Ryan T. Anderson, and Robert P. George articulated this argument rigorously in their widely discussed work What Is Marriage? Man and Woman: A Defense (2012), arguing that the revisionist view of marriage — as essentially an emotional union recognized by the state — provides no principled basis for limiting marriage to two persons, for requiring sexual exclusivity, or for treating it as presumptively permanent. If marriage is merely the legal recognition of a committed romantic relationship, there is no coherent reason to restrict it to couples rather than groups, or to insist on its permanence.

III. The Interests and Rights of Children

A. Children's Right to a Mother and a Father

A substantial body of research suggests that children, on average, fare best when raised by their married biological mother and father. This finding is consistent across studies measuring educational outcomes, emotional health, behavioral development, poverty rates, and involvement with the criminal justice system. The work of scholars such as Mark Regnerus, Douglas Allen, and Sara McLanahan (whose research on family structure long predates the same-sex marriage debate) has consistently shown the advantages of intact, biological, two-parent households.

The intact biological family provides children with something unique: a relationship with both the man and the woman responsible for their existence, access to both maternal and paternal models of love and authority, and a genetic and relational continuity that adopted or donor-conceived children often spend lifetimes seeking.

By redefining marriage, the law declares — as a matter of public principle — that it makes no difference whether a child is raised by both a mother and a father, or by two mothers, or by two fathers. This is, at minimum, an unproven assertion, and at worst a falsehood elevated to legal doctrine. The law should not enshrine an experiment on children as a constitutional right.

B. The Commodification Concerns

The normalization of same-sex marriage inevitably increases reliance on assisted reproduction technologies and surrogacy arrangements that raise profound ethical concerns. Surrogacy, in particular, involves the contractual use of women's bodies for reproduction — a practice that much of Europe, including progressive nations like France and Germany, has banned or heavily restricted on feminist and human-rights grounds. Donor conception deliberately severs the connection between biological parentage and family, creating children who are, by design, denied knowledge of or relationship with one biological parent.

When the law redefines marriage to include unions that are inherently non-procreative, it implicitly endorses and encourages these arrangements, treating the creation of motherless or fatherless families not as an unfortunate necessity but as a positive good equivalent to the natural family. The interests of adults in forming recognized relationships should not override the interests of children in knowing and being raised by their biological parents wherever possible.

IV. Religious Liberty and the Consequences of Redefinition

A. The Emerging Conflicts

Proponents of same-sex marriage frequently assured the public that its legalization would have no effect on those who disagreed. This assurance has proven hollow. Since Obergefell, individuals and institutions that maintain a traditional view of marriage have faced mounting legal, economic, and professional consequences:

  • Small business owners — bakers, florists, photographers, and wedding venue operators — have been subjected to lawsuits, fines, and the loss of their livelihoods for declining to participate in same-sex wedding ceremonies that violate their religious convictions. The cases of Jack Phillips (Masterpiece Cakeshop), Barronelle Stutzman (Arlene's Flowers), and others represent real people who were punished not for refusing to serve gay customers in general, but for declining to participate in a specific ceremony.

  • Religious adoption and foster care agencies — including Catholic Charities in multiple cities — have been forced to close or to violate their religious mission by being required to place children with same-sex couples as a condition of their operating licenses or government contracts.

  • Educational institutions with traditional marriage requirements for faculty and staff housing have come under pressure from accreditation bodies, state regulators, and federal agencies.

  • Individuals in professions such as counseling, public service, and academia have been disciplined or dismissed for expressing traditional views about marriage.

The promise that same-sex marriage would simply "expand" marriage without affecting anyone else was always implausible. When the state declares same-sex and opposite-sex unions to be identical in the eyes of the law, it simultaneously declares that the traditional view — held by every major world religion and the vast majority of human beings throughout history — is the equivalent of racial bigotry. The cultural and legal logic of Obergefell is inherently coercive toward dissenters.

B. The First Freedom

Religious liberty is not a secondary concern or a niche interest — it is the first freedom enumerated in the Bill of Rights. The American republic was founded, in significant part, by people fleeing religious coercion. When the redefinition of marriage puts the state on a collision course with the sincere religious convictions of tens of millions of citizens — Catholic, Evangelical Protestant, Orthodox Jewish, Muslim, Latter-day Saint, and others — something has gone gravely wrong.

Restoring the traditional legal definition of marriage would eliminate the root cause of these conflicts, allowing those who support same-sex relationships to do so freely in their private and civic lives while removing the legal mechanism that compels dissenters to affirm what their consciences forbid.

V. The Slippery Slope Is Not a Fallacy

Critics once dismissed as alarmist the warning that redefining marriage to include same-sex couples would provide no logical stopping point. Yet the very arguments used to justify same-sex marriage — that marriage is fundamentally about love, commitment, and the recognition of intimate relationships — apply equally to polygamous and polyamorous arrangements. If the conjugal understanding of marriage (a comprehensive union between man and woman oriented toward procreation) is abandoned, there is no principled basis on which to maintain the limitation to two persons.

Since Obergefell, legal and cultural advocacy for the recognition of polyamorous relationships and plural marriage has accelerated. Municipalities such as Somerville and Cambridge, Massachusetts, have extended legal recognition to polyamorous domestic partnerships. Academic journals and mainstream media have published increasingly sympathetic treatments of plural relationships. The logical trajectory of the revisionist understanding of marriage is not speculative — it is already unfolding.

Restoring the conjugal definition of marriage does not merely preserve a tradition; it preserves the coherence and intelligibility of a vital legal category. Without the grounding principle of sexual complementarity and procreative orientation, "marriage" becomes an infinitely flexible label that the state attaches to whatever relationships currently enjoy political favor — which is to say, it ceases to mean anything at all.

VI. The Path Forward: Democratic Restoration, Not Animus

It is essential to emphasize that the case for restoring the traditional definition of marriage is not a case against the dignity, worth, or civil rights of gay and lesbian Americans. Every person, regardless of sexual orientation, possesses inherent human dignity and is entitled to the full protection of the law against violence, discrimination in employment and housing, and unjust treatment by the state.

The argument, rather, is that marriage is a specific institution with a specific nature and purpose, and that redefining it by judicial fiat has caused real legal harm — to the Constitution, to democratic self-governance, to religious liberty, and to the normative understanding that children deserve, wherever possible, both a mother and a father.

The appropriate remedy is legislative and democratic. States should be free to establish civil union or domestic partnership frameworks that extend relevant legal protections — hospital visitation, inheritance rights, insurance benefits, and similar provisions — to same-sex couples, while reserving the institution of marriage for the conjugal union of husband and wife. This approach honors both the principle of equal treatment and the principle that marriage has a distinct meaning rooted in nature and the common good.

Conclusion

The redefinition of marriage in Obergefell v. Hodges was a constitutional error of the first order — a decision in which five justices imposed their moral convictions on three hundred million citizens, overriding the democratic process, distorting the Constitution, and setting in motion a cascade of conflicts between civil law and religious liberty. The traditional understanding of marriage as the union of man and woman is not an artifact of bigotry; it is an institution grounded in human nature, recognized across civilizations, and oriented toward the most vital task any society faces: the creation and formation of the next generation.

Restoring this definition would not diminish the dignity of any person. It would reaffirm the principle that the meaning of our most fundamental institutions should be determined by the people through democratic deliberation, not imposed by judicial decree. It would reassert that children's interests — not adults' desires for validation — should be at the center of marriage law. And it would resolve the growing conflicts between the state and the millions of citizens whose religious convictions will not permit them to affirm what they believe to be untrue.

A free society can tolerate deep disagreements about the nature of marriage. What it cannot tolerate indefinitely is the use of state power to enforce one side's answer and to punish the other. 1. Marriage is not an arbitrary legal construct. It is a pre-political institution the law recognizes, not invents.

For millennia, across cultures, religions, and political systems that agreed on little else, marriage has meant the same thing: the comprehensive union of male and female. Only the union of a man and a woman can naturally produce children, and every society depends on that union to produce the next generation and to bind those children to the two people responsible for bringing them into the world.

Civil marriage law exists primarily to channel that procreative reality into a stable social institution. The state has no compelling reason to regulate friendships, romantic partnerships, or love in general. It has an overwhelming reason to regulate and incentivize the relationship that can create children and provide them with both a mother and a father. By redefining marriage to include same-sex unions, the law severed marriage from its core public purpose and turned it into a government certificate of emotional validation.

Restoring the traditional definition restores coherence. It says the law recognizes marriage because it matters for society in a way that other relationships, however meaningful to the individuals involved, simply do not.

Social science and common sense converge on one point: children do best when raised by their married biological mother and father in a low-conflict home. No one denies that many same-sex couples love and care for children, or that many children in other family forms thrive. But as a matter of public policy and aspirational norm, the state should privilege the family form that connects children to both halves of their ancestry and provides complementary maternal and paternal models of nurture.

Even many legal scholars who support same-sex marriage as a policy matter have criticized Obergefell as flawed jurisprudence. Nothing in the text, history, or tradition of the Fourteenth Amendment requires a state to redefine marriage. For most of American history, marriage law was understood to be within the police powers reserved to the states and the people.

In a functioning constitutional republic, profound social changes should be made through persuasion, debate, and votes — not by five unelected justices imposing their moral vision on 320 million Americans. In 2015, dozens of states had recently voted, often by large majorities, to preserve the traditional definition of marriage. Obergefell nullified all of those votes overnight.

It would return the question to where it belongs: the state legislatures, and ultimately the people. Some states would legalize it, some would not, and that pluralistic outcome is precisely how federalism is supposed to handle deeply contested moral questions. Restoring democratic debate is more legitimate and more stable than preserving a judicial fiat.
